stories.headline: Could Malaysia return to F1 calendar? The state of play despite Sepang travel chaos
stories.summary: Malaysia's Sepang circuit hosted a popular -- and, as it stands, one-off -- return to the Formula 1 calendar, although it was overshadowed by three days of travel chaos and nightmare experiences for fans.
stories.body:
Malaysia's Sepang circuit hosted a popular -- and, as it stands, one-off -- return to the Formula 1 calendar, although it was overshadowed by three days of travel chaos and nightmare experiences for fans.

The race itself delivered an entertaining spectacle full of incident, albeit after a demonstration of the worst part of F1's new V6 turbo hybrid engines. So where has its stand-in appearance as the Bahrain Grand Prix left it in terms of returning in the future?

After the race, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim confirmed discussions with F1 about the likelihood of the nation becoming a regular F1 host again.

"Had the opportunity to hold a meeting with the President who also serves as the Chief Executive Officer of Formula 1, Stefano Domenicali, before the race began at the Sepang International Circuit," he posted on X. "We discussed the prospects of reinstating the Malaysia Grand Prix permanently in the Formula 1 calendar, thereby fulfilling the long-standing desire of fans who have eagerly awaited its return to Sepang. However, this effort will require time because arranging the race calendar must take into account the packed schedule as well as existing contractual commitments with host countries."

- Max Verstappen wins disrupted Bahrain GP, Kimi Antonelli extends title lead as George Russell retires

- Bahrain GP was the worst indictment of F1's new engine regs yet

- George Russell on Bahrain GP retirement: 'Beyond disappointment' as title chances all but over

Sources with knowledge of the calendar have told ESPN that any deal with Sepang will be a long way off as things stand, but there is clearly renewed energy behind the circuit's viability as a race host. F1 boss Domenicali often says there's a long waiting list of venues who are hoping to get an event of their own and he's not wrong.

Sources have told ESPN Sepang has put itself into Formula 1's good graces by accommodating the Bahrain event -- which will help the sport keep its commercial obligation of not dropping below 22 events in 2026 -- but that also does not mean it has automatically shot to the top of any waiting or priority list

One well-placed paddock source told ESPN that, given the current F1 deals in existence, the earliest Sepang could come back to the race calendar would be 2030, a timeline Sepang officials would not confirm or deny when asked on record. The official line all weekend, until the prime minister's comments, that all focus was on the 2026 event. But a lot needs to happen for any deal beyond that to gather pace.

Finances will be the biggest obstacle. Bahrain stumped up most if not all of the reported $50 million hosting fee for this year's event. Without that, there's no chance Sepang could have been a 2027 fallback option, it wasn't sat around with a bucketload of cash just waiting for an opportunity to host a race if needed.The venue dropped off the calendar in 2017 because it could not afford F1's hosting fees as they were then -- an influx of new races this side of the pandemic has escalated the average fee even more, with F1 enjoying a commercial boom it has never experienced before.

But one thing was clear from Sunday's event: the appetite for the sport in Malaysia is bigger than ever. A lack of fan interest in a fallow time for F1 killed the event off a decade ago: demand appears to be well and truly back now and that might help the circuit in its bid to find the financial backing it would need to even have a shot at having a seat at the table in future.

Why was the fan experience so bad?

One of the standout moments ​of Sepang's weekend was the loud roar from the fans when Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton made crucial passes during the race -- Malaysia's fanbase was always loud and over 110,000 people were in attendance for raceday alone.

Many of them will have endured a lot to have seen those overtakes.

Because Sepang's event was the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Bahrain's race organisers took control of all elements of the event -- it flew in meat for the paddock, local ice cream vendors, over 500 event marshals, and even organised its Gulf Air Dreamliner to fly over the grid (even in the middle of a deluge of rain) to keep its prerace tradition alive. It was the equivalent of someone leasing out a friend's house for a party, but telling them they would deal with every single facet of the event.

The fact that it was Bahrain and not Malaysia involved in planning every detail, plus the number of people in attendance, caused problems.

- Lewis Hamilton: No plans to visit casino with Ferrari strategists after slick tyre gamble

- Max Verstappen praises Red Bull on 'very special' Bahrain Grand Prix win after 'tough start to year'

"We're not used to this," Bahrain International Circuit chief executive Sheikh Salman bin Isa Al Khalifa told ESPN ahead of the weekend. "It's not like we have experience in those numbers."

Bahrain's infrastructure is usually built around an event which caters for 55,000 fans a day, but the attendance was double that every day. The grandstand along the start-finish line alone held 35,000 fans. Bahraini officials were not only dealing with a completely unfamiliar circuit and external road system but an influx of fans they simply do not deal with at their Sakhir equivalent.

Anyone travelling into the circuit could see that the people organising this year's event were overwhelmed. From Friday onwards, there were reports of fans having to walk up to 11 kilometers home because shuttles had simply stopped without warning immediately after sessions finished. ESPN saw hoards of people walking down the motorway's hard shoulder on all three days of the event, noticeably at its worst on Friday but bad every day.

Things compounded the problem, like the Grab and Bolt exclusion zone stopping rideshare companies from getting anywhere near the venue. Once fans got into the venue, they found progress getting anywhere slow. Queues for grandstand gates were slow, queues for concessions stands even slower.

F1 photographer Kym Illman extensively covered the chaos within the circuit on his video channels -- he reported plastic water bottles being banned on entry (fans then had to buy bottled water inside the venue) and long lines of up to an hour for water refill stations, many of which ran out of water early in the event, and there were reports of 50 ambulances being sent into the circuit on Friday alone for people who had passed out in the humid conditions.

Videos from Saturday's DJ Axwell concert on Saturday -- in a field which was supposed to accommodate 10,000 people -- had upwards of 50,000 people in attendance, with many leaving the venue either during qualifying or immediately after qualifying having heard horror stories from the day before. It caused an almighty bottleneck outside the circuit and many fans were left stranded in no man's land -- unable to get anywhere, but also not allowed to return inside the circuit -- for hours on end in the stifling Malaysia heat.

This appeared to have caused similar on Sunday, with various reports on social media of fans leaving before the end of the race to try and avoid similar chaos, but still getting back to their hotels 10 or 11 hours later. It all left a sour taste for many and overshadowed what was otherwise a popular return for one of F1's great venues of its more recent past.

Who was to blame was an open question -- many in attendance pointed the finger at Bahrain's organisers, who appeared to have underestimated the logistical challenge of putting on a race at a venue many of them had never visited before, but the eight-week turnaround from the announcement to the event did not help.

Sources have told ESPN that F1 would have intervened and made tweaks to basic things such as motorway signage had there been more time to properly come up with a plan of action -- most events are meticulously planned and mapped out for months in advance, and many of them do not go ahead without problems anyway. Local Malaysian police also seemed slightly overwhelmed by the amount of traffic outside the circuit, especially on Friday and Saturday.

That might all be simplified should Sepang host the event itself in future -- the venue regularly holds a MotoGP event without similar issues and it seems as though a perfect storm of things contributed to the bad time a lot of fans experienced across the three days.

stories.headline: UFC 332 takeaways: Talbott, Silva validate their top billing
stories.summary: Payton Talbott finished another former champion in Deiveson Figueiredo on a night full of knockouts at UFC 332.
stories.body:
The options were plenty for performance bonuses after UFC 332 in Salt Lake City. The fight card set a UFC record for knockouts with 11, and nine came in the first round. The most resounding KO went to men's bantamweight Payton Talbott in the co-main event. He came out strong, sending former champion Deiveson Figueiredo to the canvas twice before finishing him a little over two minutes into the fight. The win is Talbott's second in a row over a former champion and likely means big things ahead for him, but the loss for Figueiredo doesn't do anything to minimize his legacy in the UFC.

The main event, which received prefight chatter over whether it was worthy of a headlining slot, was high energy but mostly one-sided. Natalia Silva, the No. 1 women's flyweight contender, earned her first UFC championship with a unanimous decision over Wang Cong. The 29-year-old joins men's flyweight Joshua Van as the only UFC champions under 30.

Was the main event criticism validated?
The UFC took heat on social media for booking Silva vs. Wang in a main event on a numbered card. Silva was at the front of a long line of women's flyweight title contenders, no question, but it's fair to say Wang, unranked by ESPN and outside the top five in the UFC's own rankings, jumped the queue.

But while I'm on board with a lot of the criticism the UFC receives for its matchmaking, especially at a championship level, I understand what the fight promotion was going for in this case: The UFC was trying to set up a couple of possible storylines involving Valentina Shevchenko, who vacated the women's flyweight title to make the Silva-Wang title fight a possibility after suffering an undisclosed injury that will sideline her for "up to one year."

Why Wang? She might not have an extensive UFC résumé, but she beat Shevchenko in a kickboxing match in 2015. Their history is not unlike that of Alex Pereira and Israel Adesanya, who met twice in kickboxing, with Pereira winning both and knocking out Adesanya in one of those fights. It provided a setup for their UFC rivalry.

A Wang vs. Shevchenko angle became moot, as things turned out, because Silva was too much for the Chinese fighter to handle. Wang came in with a 10-1 MMA record, but she had zero fights against top-10 flyweights, and it showed. Silva, by contrast, came in having defeated former UFC champions (Jessica Andrade, Alexa Grasso and Rose Namajunas) in each of her past three fights.

Silva was too fast, too elusive and too precise with her punches and kicks. Wang had no answers, looked lost and couldn't get her offense going until the fifth round, when it was too late. Not to vindicate the prefight matchmaking criticism, but this sure was a lopsided and not-so-fiery bout, one that got booed by a crowd that had been treated to a UFC-record 11 knockouts on the night.

So now the 125-pound division is left with the Silva vs. Shevchenko storyline we were expecting to see before Shevchenko was injured. It will be interesting to see how Silva's speed holds up when she meets her predecessor with the belt, and how differently she'll fight when up against an opponent with a strong grappling game. Oddly, that wasn't even addressed in Silva's postfight interview in the cage. Shevchenko's name wasn't even mentioned. Now, that is a UFC decision worth questioning. -- Jeff Wagenheim

Quick thanks to Figueiredo

MMA loves to move quickly, and it's ready to move very fast with Talbott. Talbott is everything MMA could want in a prospect, and his future is very bright.

So before we all take off on the Talbott train (as we inevitably will), let's take a moment to shout out one of the most exciting flyweights of all time, Figueiredo.

Let's be honest, Figueiredo was always a borrowed bantamweight. He struggled to make 125 pounds, and most of the sport was happy to see him ditch the weight cut in 2023, but he was also undersized at 135.

It's easy to forget now, as UFC men's flyweight champion Van has taken the sport by storm -- but the flyweight division was still in a precarious position when Figueiredo made his mark in 2020. Henry Cejudo saved the division by knocking out TJ Dillashaw in 2018, but then eventually vacated a weight class the UFC seriously considered shutting down. Figueiredo picked up where Cejudo left off, saving the division with his one-punch knockout power and (frankly) villain charisma. He played the role of "bad guy" in his back-to-back fights against Joseph Benavidez in 2020, as well as his four-fight rivalry with Brandon Moreno.

It was inevitable when he moved up in weight, but for a three-year period, Figueiredo was the exact figure the flyweight division needed. The 38-year-old's career is undoubtedly coming to an end soon, but Figueiredo was not just a terrific fighter and champion in his prime, he will forever be remembered as a significant hero of flyweight MMA. -- Brett Okamoto

stories.headline: USMNT's young stars shine to give Pochettino 'fantastic problem'
stories.summary: USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino said that the number of players performing at a high level is "a fantastic problem to have" after teenagers Cavan Sullivan and Julian Hall propelled the USMNT to 3-0 win over rivals Mexico on Saturday.
stories.body:
GLENDALE, Ariz. -- United States men's national team coach Mauricio Pochettino said that the number of players performing at a high level is "a fantastic problem to have" after teenagers Cavan Sullivan and Julian Hall propelled the USMNT to 3-0 win over rivals Mexico on Saturday.

The U.S. endured a difficult first half, and scored completely against the run of play in the 28th minute when Hall converted from close range after Mexico keeper Raúl Rangel spilled Gio Reyna's low cross right in front of goal.

- Cavan Sullivan has arrived: U.S. phenom's goal caps a memorable win over Mexico

- Márquez bemoans 'terrible mistakes' as Mexico humbled by USMNT

- USMNT player ratings: Sullivan, Hall 9/10 in big win vs. Mexico

The USMNT began to make more headway in the second half, and doubled its lead in the 62nd minute when Sullivan intercepted a pass from Rangel, and chipped the ball into the net from 35 yards out. The match lost its edge when Mexico's Mateo Chávez was red carded in the 67th minute following a scrap with Sebastian Berhalter.

Malik Tillman finished off the scoring in the 84th minute, latching onto another wayward Mexico pass to firing into the net.

Hall, 18, is just the third USMNT player to score in his first three national team appearances, while 17-year-old Sullivan became the youngest scorer in USMNT history.

"I think it's a fantastic problem for us," Pochettino said about the performances of his team's young players. "I think we will take the right decision in the right moment, but I think it's a very good problem to see.

"Now it's not a moment at all, but yes, we appreciate that situation and of course hope that we will be in that situation that young players perform in the way that they deserve to be with us."

Pochettino also pronounced himself pleased with the way his side weathered Mexico's early pressure.

"I think that this, overall, was a great opportunity to discover ourself, to see ourselves in a difficult game with a very good team. Again, Mexico is a great team," Pochettino said.

"Yes, I think two different maybe halves. The first half I think Mexico started really well. They forced us to play back. We never connected. We were losing all the duels. And then we start to grow after 15, 20 minutes. And I think it was a good lesson the first half because it was the sense of work all together, suffer together even when you are not playing well in the way that you plan to play."

But Pochettino couldn't help but admire the performance of Sullivan, who impressed with his work on both sides the ball.

"I think he's a talented player with enormous quality, but with a very good balance, in possession and out of possession," Pochettino said about Sullivan. "He's a fighter, he's a warrior. It's difficult to find this type of player with a tremendous quality.

"And then I think Cavan showed in possession with the ball on the field [and] when he need to be chasing people and recover the ball. That is my impression after maybe three weeks together. And that is unbelievable, to have a player like this. I think it's a fantastic news for USA. Hope that continues in that way."

Pochettino was careful to laud Sullivan's young teammates as well, who have largely impressed during this window.

"It's a big moment because we need to be right with them," Pochettino said about the win, and the path forward. "We need to protect them. We need to support them. Our responsibility now is that this group of talented players grow in the right direction."

stories.headline: Uncapped NRL trio picked in England's World Cup squad
stories.summary: Ben Talty, Hugo Savala and Max King headline a new-look England squad for the Rugby League World Cup.
stories.body:
Brisbane prop Ben Talty, Canterbury front-rower Max King and Sydney Roosters utility Hugo Savala have been named in England's Rugby League World Cup squad.

Talty and Savala both qualify through ancestry and join Huddersfield-born King in a side assembled by Brian McDermott which contains 10 NRL players.

Savala's Roosters teammate Victor Radley is included along with Newcastle winger Dominic Young and the Dolphins duo of Morgan Knowles and Herbie Farnworth.

Canberra's Perth-bound prop Morgan Smithies has earned selection along with Wests Tigers backrower Kai Pearce-Paul and Gold Coast fullback AJ Brimson, who debuted for England in last year's Ashes whitewash.

McDermott, who is an assistant at the Titans and previously won the Super League title with Leeds, has taken over from Shaun Wane since the 3-0 series defeat.

Leeds halfback Jake Connor -- winner of last year's Man of Steel and controversially left out of the 2025 Ashes -- has again missed the cut, with McDermott preferring Hull KR playmaker Mikey Lewis.

McDermott said: "We have selected the squad after a thorough and deliberate process, underpinned by a unique decentralised preparation model that has allowed us to work closely with the players well before they come together in camp.

"Throughout that process, we have challenged players to develop a deeper understanding of themselves - their strengths, their point of difference, the areas they need to improve and the standards required to perform at international level."

England will kick off against Tonga on October 17 before also facing France and Papua New Guinea in the group stage.

England squad: Matty Ashton, AJ Brimson, Ben Currie, Zach Eckersley, Herbie Farnworth, Ethan Havard, Max King, Morgan Knowles, Mikey Lewis, Jez Litten, Junior Nsemba, Brad O'Neill, Kai Pearce-Paul, Victor Radley, Hugo Savala, Harry Smith, Morgan Smithies, Luke Thompson, Sam Walters, Ben Talty, Jack Welsby, George Williams, Dom Young.
